title: Vandesteene Breaks Through in Monaco as Keisner Cuts the Championship to Four Points
meta: Published: 14 June 2026 | By Elena Vasquez, Chief Race Correspondent | F1CC News
caption: Wesley Vandesteene celebrates his first victory of 2026 — a masterclass in survival around the streets of Monte Carlo.
body:
The Mediterranean sun was a warm, steady hand on the principality, the harbour glittering with yachts and the grandstands humming with the low, expectant murmur that only Monaco can produce. When the chequered flag fell after a race that had been torn apart and stitched back together by a red flag, it was Wesley Vandesteene who stood at the top of the podium, the Belgian having delivered a victory of patience, opportunism, and a restart so sharp it cut the field in half. Behind him, Jason Roy had started from pole and finished second, the Monaco curse intact but his championship charge very much alive. Riley Swansson, in the Ferrari, completed the podium — his first of the season, a quiet vindication after weeks of scrutiny. And the championship, which had seemed to be slipping from Eetu Väisänen's grasp, tightened to a four-point thread between the Finn and the relentless Robin Keisner.

The race had been a slow burn, the opening laps a procession of warm tyres and careful braking, until the walls began to bite. The first casualty was Richard Hicks, the Audi driver locking up at Sainte Dévote on the opening lap and spearing into the barriers. He limped back to the pits with a shattered front wing, his race effectively over before it had begun. The safety car was deployed, and the field breathed again, but the damage had been done — not just to Hicks' car, but to the rhythm of the race. From that moment on, Monaco was a game of survival.

Eetu Väisänen, starting second, had been poised to extend his championship lead. But a mechanical issue — a brake pedal that went soft and a vibration that shook the steering wheel — turned his afternoon into a test of endurance. He reported the problem early, his voice tight over the radio, and his lap times began to bleed. His teammate Riley Swansson, freed from the pressure of the championship fight, drove cleanly and stayed out of trouble, gradually climbing from fourth on the grid to third at the flag. It was Swansson's first podium of the year, and his radio silence after the race was broken only by a quiet message from the Ferrari pit wall.

The midfield was a restless swarm, and it was Quarter Kevu who cut through it with the most aggression. The reigning champion, starting 17th, made a series of daring overtakes — including a carbon-copy move at Turn 3 that he used three times to dispatch Maradóner, Konstantaras, and a recovering Hicks. But his race, so full of promise, ended in the wall. An ERS issue that had been flagged early finally betrayed him under braking for the chicane, and his Racing Bulls car snapped sideways into the barriers, sparking a safety car that would prove decisive. Kevu climbed out, his helmet still on, and stood for a moment behind the barriers, staring at the sea. His streak of consecutive points finishes — stretching back to Abu Dhabi last year — was over.

That safety car, on lap 62, was the turning point. The field bunched, and the strategists on the pit wall were forced to make choices with incomplete information. Some stopped for fresh tyres; others stayed out, gambling on a long final stint. The red flag that followed — triggered by a multi-car pile-up at the chicane after Afonso Cachinho locked up and collected Hicks and Aygen — reset the race entirely. Cachinho, the only driver on the grid yet to score a point in 2026, had been running in the points when his Haas snapped under braking. He slid into the side of Hicks' Audi, which in turn pushed Eren Aygen into the wall. All three were out. The red flag was immediate, and the remaining fourteen drivers were left with a standing restart and a sprint to the finish.

The restart, on lap 66, was where Vandesteene seized his moment. Jason Roy had led from pole and controlled the race with the authority of a man who knew the curse of Monaco — no polesitter had won here in years — but Vandesteene's launch was perfect, his Mercedes hooking up on the soft tyres and surging past the Red Bull before Sainte Dévote. The Belgian, who had started fifth, was now leading the Monaco Grand Prix, and he would not look back. The gap stretched to two seconds, then three, and Roy could do nothing but watch the silver car disappear into the tunnel.

Behind them, the race was a frenzy of DRS trains and late lunges. Sam Fact, the hero of Canada, drove from 18th on the grid to sixth, passing Väisänen with a move of pure tenacity on the hill before Casino Square. Maikel Zwart, who had spent the afternoon arguing with his team over strategy and tyre choices, finished seventh, his Mercedes finally delivering a clean result. Joshua Nathanial, still chasing points after a disastrous qualifying, climbed to ninth. And Robin Keisner, the championship challenger, nursed his Audi to fourth place, his radio message after the flag a mixture of relief and reflection. "And that's P4," his engineer told him. Keisner's reply was triumphant: "What a strategy guys and what a race, after Miami I thought our championship was over. I hope Aygen and Hicks are okay after that crash."

The tweets that followed told their own stories. Sarah Springfield, who had been running in the points before contact with Julian Kondra left her car with damage she described as "****** six ways from Sunday," had been forced to retire. She posted later: "Rollercoaster of emotions this weekend doesn't begin to describe it, shame it ended the way it did. Failed overtake on Kondra into Casino Square and got damage from it, and it forced us to retire. Onto Barcelona we go." The crash with Kondra had been a racing incident — the Alpine and the Aston Martin touching as Springfield tried to squeeze through a gap that closed. She limped back to the pits, her race over, but her words carried no bitterness, only the weariness of a driver who knows that Monaco gives and takes without mercy.

Robin Keisner's own tweet, later that evening, was triumphant: "P4 in Monaco!!! An important result that brings me back into the championship fight. Unbelievable what me and the team achieved. Up to Barcelona we go." The gap between him and Väisänen was now just four points — 102 to 98 — the Finn having salvaged eighth after his mechanical woes. Väisänen had driven through the pain, his Ferrari limping but still running, and the four points he scored felt like a victory of their own. But the momentum had shifted. Keisner, who had been 19th in 2024, 17th in 2025, now stood on the brink of leading the championship for the second time this season. The paddock, so accustomed to Ferrari's early dominance, was now witnessing a different kind of story — one of quiet resilience and relentless accumulation.

The championship table, still flickering with the aftershocks of the race, showed Väisänen on 102 points, Keisner on 98. Eren Aygen, who had crashed out and scored nothing, remained third on 92. Vandesteene's win vaulted him to fourth on 77, level with Zhao Lei. Jason Roy, despite his second place, sat sixth on 72. The constructors' battle was equally extraordinary: Ferrari led with 122 points, but Williams were level on 122, and Audi were just one point behind on 121. McLaren and Red Bull and Mercedes were locked in their own tight contest behind, while Racing Bulls and Alpine scrapped for the midfield positions. The circus heads now to Barcelona, where the heat will be different, the corners faster, and the championship fight even more unforgiving. The Mediterranean sea sparkled in the evening light, the same light that had bathed the track through every twist of a race that will be remembered for its chaos, its courage, and its quiet coronation of a new prince of Monaco.
